newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Army denies split over Serbian demonstrations.
newsitem.headline: Army denies split over Serbian demonstrations.

text.p: The Yugoslav Army denied on Monday that it was split over President Slobodan Milosevic's attempts to quell street protests against socialist rule in Serbia by using riot police to beat demonstrators.
But an army statement, stressing its unity, made no pledge of loyalty to Milosevic who has struggled for six weeks to contain protests that have paralysed Belgrade for more than six hours every day.
In an ominous turn to the confict, unidentified officers warned Milosevic at the weekend that their troops would not fire on demonstrators and could turn against him.
The army statement did not mention that threat but admitted attempts were under way to persuade the army to act unconstitutionally.

The dissidents apparently included men of the elite 63rd Paratroop Brigade, based in the southern city of Nis, and other garrisons who wrote to Milosevic, army commander General Momcilo Perisic and Nis students.
The letter was unsigned and unauthenticated and there was no indication of the strength of the rebels.

But genuine or not, it underlined the disarray in the socialist government and Milosevic's difficulty in coping with a crisis which political analysts say is making his future more uncertain every day.
A split in the army would doom any attempt by him to declare a state of emergency or pit the army against Serbian police forces whose own loyalty is doubtful.

The army helped Milosevic put down demonstrations in 1991 but has remained neutral during his conflict with the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition since it was cheated by the socialists of victory in local elections on November 17.
Political sources said a copy of the letter was handed to Perisic when he met paratroop officers in Nis during a tour of major garrisons to test the army's mood.
According to newspaper reports, Perisic was told the army would disobey any order to open fire on civilians.
The letter urged him to "muster the courage, of which you once had plenty" and side with opposition attempts to win democratic reforms that would end one-party rule in Serbia.
Perisic was reported to have told Milosevic earlier in the crisis that the army would not help him but the officers' letter said dissidents were ready to go further.

"We will not allow Serbia to go under, we shall never act against our own people," the text said. "if necessary, we shall place ourselves at the head of the Serbian people in the final victory of truth."
The letter was not addressed to Zajedno and included a warning to the opposition that it would be toppled in its turn if it did not behave democratically in power.
The army has its own grievances against Milosevic who humiliated it at the expense of the police after the war against Croatian secession from former Yugoslavia in 1991/92.
Scores of generals were summarily purged and the army was run down while the police were reinforced with extra men and military fire power.

The letter was couched as a message to Milosevic "from the officers whom you denigrated so much and tried to turn into minor figures in this country, whom you denigrated in the 1991/92 war for which you bear part of the responsibility."

The ill-feeling against him did not prevent the army helping the Serb side in the Bosnian war when it provided the Bosnian Serb Army with a steady flow of arms, equipment and fuel to fight the former Yugoslav republic's Moslem and Croat-led independence.
It has remained strong enough to prevent Milosevic extraditing indicted Yugoslav and Bosnian Serb army officers for trial by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.
In former Yugoslavia, the army had quasi-independent status and was known as a "state within a state" which ran an exporting arms industry as well acting as a guarantor of communist rule.
